translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil concerning the wrathful.
Just as the instructions of physicians, when they are carried out well and with skill, show their benefit after they have been tested, so it is also with spiritual instructions.
For when practice bears witness to the commandments, then their wisdom and their benefit become evident, for the perfecting of those who obey them.
For we have heard the "Proverbs of Solomon," how they cry out openly:
"Wrath destroys even the wise." And again we have heard the teaching of the Apostle, which says:
"Put all wrath and anger and clamor far from you," as befits the saints. And the Lord says:
"Whoever becomes angry with his brother without cause is liable to judgment."
But now, when we have come to know this passion by experience, a passion that did not arise among us but came upon us from outside,
like an unexpected gust of wind, then we have understood the wonder of the divine commandments.
When we gave way to wrath, as one gives an outlet to a violent river,
and quietly watched the ugly turmoil of those seized by this passion, we came to know in actual fact the truth of the word of Solomon, who says:
"A wrathful man is not comely." For once this passion has darkened the mind and seized the power of the soul itself,
it turns a person wholly into a beast and does not even allow him to remain within human nature, since he no longer has the help of reason.
For as venom is present in venomous reptiles, so anger is present in the wrathful: they bark like dogs, they strike like scorpions, they bite like snakes.
Scripture too knows how to call those seized by this passion by the names of those beasts
to which they have likened themselves through their wickedness, for Scripture names them mad dogs and snakes, offspring of vipers.
For those who are ready to harm their neighbor and to do evil to one another are rightly counted with poisonous snakes, which by nature have an implacable hatred of human beings.
Through anger tongues become unbridled, mouths unguarded, and hands unrestrained;
insults and reproaches and slanders and blows, and the other evils beyond number, are all the offspring of anger and wrath.

Through anger swords are sharpened, and the death of a human being comes about by a human hand; through it brothers have failed to recognize one another, and parents and children have forgotten nature.
For the angry first fail to recognize themselves, and then all their friends as well.
For as a violent torrent, rushing down a ravine, carries away everything it finds before it,
so are the impulses of the angry: violent and uncontrollable, they rush upon all alike.
Before the angry neither elders are honored, nor virtue of life, nor the bond of kinship, nor good deeds done in the past, nor anything else worthy of honor.
Anger is madness, for some bring many evils even upon themselves, when in their eagerness to do evil to another they neglect themselves.
For just as by an evil passion, so they are goaded by the memory of the one who has afflicted them, and their anger rages within them and leaps up.
And they do not subside until they have repaid the evil to the one who afflicted them, and perhaps they themselves receive a greater evil,
just as those who have fallen from great heights often suffer more than they inflict, when they are shattered by striking against objects that stand in their way.
Who could tell the evils of wrath?
How the wrathful are inflamed by a slight cause, shout and turn savage, and assail others no less fiercely than some venomous [?], and they do not rest
until, through some great evil, their wrath bursts like a bubble of water and that inflamed anger goes out.
For neither sword nor fire nor any other terrible thing is enough to restrain a soul maddened by anger, any more
than it can restrain the demon-possessed, from whom the wrathful differ in nothing, neither in appearance nor in mind.
For when they desire to do evil, the blood of the heart boils up, like the violent force of a fire,
blazing and fierce, and the inner aspect comes out on the outside as well, and the enraged person changes into another appearance and no longer has his former appearance,
as when people on the stage are changed into another guise.
And their eyes are no longer their own natural ones, but they stare like a madman's and turn the color of fire, and they sharpen their teeth like boars going into battle.
Their face is the color of liver and the color of blood, the body swells, and the veins burst from the inner turmoil and tumult of the soul,
their voice is harsh and disorderly, and their speech is improper and comes out at random, not coming forth in an orderly and seemly way.
But when wrath carries the wrathful away into excess, like a flame fed by an abundance of fuel, then there appear deeds that words cannot express and that are unbearable to hear:

hands stretched out against a brother and going at all his limbs, and feet shamelessly kicking the parts of the body that ought to be treated with care, and everything that comes to hand becomes an instrument of that madness.
And if, through the demon, they also find their like on the opposing [?] side, then they fall upon one another and do what it is fitting to be done through such a demon.
For the wrathful receive mutilations of their limbs, and often even deaths, as the wages of wrath.
For the one makes the beginning of laying a hand on the other to do evil, and the other pays him back in return,
and again the first strikes him, and the other in turn does not put up with it, and their bodies are cut with wounds, but anger does not perceive the wounds,
for it has no leisure to notice a wound when their whole soul is roused to do evil to the one afflicting them.
But do not cure evil with evil, nor strive to outdo one another in wickedness,
for in an evil combat the one who wins is the more wretched, because he departs full of greater sin.
Do not be one who carries out that evil partnership, nor a more evil repayer of that evil debt.
But if he has grown angry and reviled you, stop the evil by silence.
But you, who take his anger into your own heart like a wave and resemble the winds,
which, by blowing in return, turn back what has come to them from another wind: do not take your enemy as your teacher, and do not do what you hate.
Do not become like a mirror of the angry man, showing his color in yourself. Is he flushed red?
But are you not purple? Are his eyes wild? But do yours look on calmly? Is his voice disorderly? But is yours orderly?
Not even a voice sent out in an uninhabited wilderness returns so wholly to the one who spoke as an insult goes back to the one who insulted.
Rather, the voice returns to the speaker just as it went out, but the insult returns to the insulter with increase.
For see how angry people hurl insults at one another?
One calls the other contemptible, of contemptible stock, and the other calls him a beggar of beggars;
this one calls him poor and that one a vagrant; this one calls him foolish and that one mad, until their insults, like arrows, run out.
When they have uttered every insult with their mouths, they then fight with their hands,
for contentiousness stirs up quarrel, and quarrel begets insult, and insults beget wounds, and wounds often bring forth death.
But let us check this evil from its very first beginning, that is, let us by every means root anger out of our souls,
for in this way we shall be able to root out many evils along with it, as along with their root and parent.
If he insults you, bless him; if he strikes you, endure it; if he spits on you and treats you with contempt, consider yourself,
that you are earth and will return to earth, for whoever fortifies himself with such thoughts will find every insult to fall short of the truth.
And if you do this, you will also make your enemy unable to do you harm,
when you show yourself to be one who despises those insults, and you will win for yourself the great crown of patience, when you take the other's madness as an occasion for wisdom.
And if you would listen to me, you would even go beyond the insult: if the other were to call you contemptible and poor and a nobody born of nobodies,
you would call yourself earth and ashes; you are not more honorable than our father Abraham, who called himself this.
Again: if he calls you foolish and a storyteller [?] and worthy of nothing, call yourself a worm,
born of dung, and no man; you are not greater than David, the great king and prophet, who said this.
Learn also the good example of the prophet Moses: when he was treated with contempt by Aaron and Miriam, he said nothing evil about them, but rather prayed to God.
Whose disciple do you wish to be? That of those holy and blessed men, or that of those filled with the evil spirit?
When the trial of insult is stirred up against you, then consider it in this way: that a judgment has come upon you.
Either you will draw near to God through long-suffering, or you will go over to the devil through anger; give your mind time to choose the good portion.
For if you practice forbearance, either you will benefit him somewhat by that example of yours,
or rather you will burn him all the more by your contempt for his insult. For what could be more painful to an enemy than when he sees his enemy standing above his insults?
Do not lower the height of your soul, and do not become a source of pleasure to those who insult you.
Let him talk in vain: such people will burst upon their own heads. For it is as if someone bore enmity against a hard rock and kept striking it:
he does not harm the rock but himself, since he does it no harm and cannot quell his anger.
So too, whoever insults a patient person finds no consolation for his passion, but rather burns the more.
And at the same time, do you see what each of you is called? For he is called an insulter and you forbearing,
he wrathful and disorderly and you patient and gentle. He will repent of the words he spoke, but you will never repent of virtue.
Why is there need of many words? Let me say briefly that this insult has shut the kingdom of heaven to him, for:
"Revilers shall not inherit the kingdom of heaven," but silence has prepared the kingdom of heaven for you, for:
"He who endures to the end shall be saved." But if you pay back in kind and become equal to the one who reviled you, what answer will you give to the Lord?
That he made the beginning of the anger? And what forgiveness does that deserve?
For not even a fornicator, if he lays the blame on another fornicator as the one who stirred up his desire for the sin, would for that reason be deemed worthy of a lesser judgment.
For no one is given a crown without an opponent, and no fall happens without a battle.
Do you not hear what David says: "When the sinner rose up before me," I did not grow angry and repay evil, but "I became deaf, I was humbled, and I kept silent even from good things"?
But you grow angry at the insult as something evil, and then in turn you imitate it as something good.
See now, you have done the very thing you detested. Or do you regard the other man's evil as good, and count your own as nothing?
Is insult evil? Then flee from it, for you will not escape judgment on the grounds that he made the beginning of that anger.
Rather, I am fully convinced that for this reason an even greater judgment will come upon you, and justly so, because
he had no model of orderly conduct set before him, whereas you saw the ugliness of the angry man. Why then did you not flee from becoming like him?
Instead you too become like him, and you are turbulent and fierce and angry, and your passion becomes a defense for that first man,
for by those deeds that you do, you free him from blame and condemn yourself all the more.
For if anger is evil, why did you not keep away from that evil?
But if it deserves forgiveness and is not very evil, why then are you angry at the angry man?
And even if you were the last to enter upon doing that evil, this is of no benefit to you,
For in wrestling, too, it is not the one who enters the arena first who receives the crown, but the one who conquers.
And likewise, not only the one who made the beginning of the evil is punished, but also the one who follows that evil example into sin.
If he has called you poor and a beggar and speaks the truth, accept that truth and take it upon yourself; but if he is lying, why have you taken that word to heart?
Never accept praise that is outside the truth, and do not become angry over an insult that does not touch you.
Do you not see how arrows, if they strike resistant materials, turn back, but on soft and yielding materials they spend their sharpness?
Of the same sort is insult as well, when it meets resistance: whoever resists it receives it into himself, but whoever lets it go and gives way,
by that softness dissolves the wickedness coming upon him. Or why does that reproach of poverty trouble you?
Remember your nature, for naked you came into this world, and naked you will also depart from here. And what is poorer than the naked?
You have heard nothing evil, if you understand yourself. Or who has ever been thrown into prison anywhere because of poverty?
For it is not poverty that is a reproach, but enduring that poverty without dignity.
Remember Christ, the King of all, for: "Though rich, he became poor for us."
Again, if he calls you foolish and uneducated, remember those insults of the Jews, with which they insulted the true Wisdom, saying:
"You are a Samaritan and there is a demon in you." And if you become angry, you have confirmed that insult, for what is more foolish than anger?
But if you remain without anger, you have put the insulter to shame, for you have shown wisdom by your deed.
If he has struck you, what wonder is it, for they struck the Lord as well. Or have you been spat upon?
But our King too was spat upon and "did not turn his face away from the shame of spitting." Or have they slandered you?
They did the same to the Judge of all as well. Or have they torn your garment? But they also stripped my Lord and divided his garment among themselves.
You still fall far short of him, for you have not yet been condemned, you have not yet been crucified; you fall far short of being like him.
Remember all this and calm your wrath, for such preparations of the mind wipe every evil from the soul and bring the mind to tranquility.
And this is surely what David was saying: "I made myself ready and was not troubled."
It is necessary, then, to calm that maddened agitation by remembering those blessed names, as the great David prayed concerning that reviler Shimei,
for he gave anger no time to stir, when he ascribed the cause of the matter to God and said:
"The Lord commanded Shimei to curse David," for he was hearing it said of him: he is a man of blood, he is a lawless man.
He was not angry with him, but humbled himself, as if that insult were coming upon him deservedly.
And so you too must wipe two things from your heart: first, that you should not consider yourself worthy of any great honor, and second,
Do not suppose that anyone among men is far beneath you in honor, and then anger will never master you at the time of insult.
For it is an evil thing if someone who has received good from you and is indebted to you for many favors should, along with his ingratitude, also become one who insults you.
This is an evil thing, but it is evil for the one who does the evil, and not for the one to whom it is done.
Let him insult you, but do not you be insulted. Let his words be a test of your wisdom. If you do not become angry, you are unharmed.
But if your soul should suffer anything, hold that grief within yourself, for it is written:
"Within me my heart was troubled," which means that the passion did not even reach the outside, but, like a wave within the shore of the sea, it was broken and subsided.
Humble for me your heart, which is boiling up and beside itself.
Let the passions be ashamed before the rational part of your nature, as the disorderliness of children is ashamed at the arrival of an honorable man.
But how are we to escape the passion of anger, except in this way: by teaching ourselves that anger must not outrun our mind?
Rather, let us strive for this, that it should never run ahead of the mind, but that we should have it like a bridled horse beneath us, and, as a horse is to the bridle,
so let it be obedient to our reason, and let it never go outside its proper order, but let it be directed by reason wherever we wish.
For that power of anger in the soul is useful to us for many virtues.
When, like a soldier who receives arms from the commander and readily puts their aid to use
against whatever he has been ordered, so it becomes a helper to you, to that rational faculty of yours, in the battle against sin.
For anger is the sinew of the soul, and it gives it strength for firmness in what is good.
For if it ever takes hold of a soul slackened by desire, as the tempering bath takes iron, it thus tempers it and makes it hard and courageous in place of that slackness.
For if you do not employ anger against the wicked one, you will not be able to hate him as is due.
For we need equal zeal for loving virtue and for hating sin, and for this anger is useful,
when, as a dog obeys the shepherd, so it obeys the mind, and wherever the mind urges it on, there it goes.

And when something profitable comes, then let it be gentle and obedient and a source of repose to the mind, and let it be savage toward a strange voice and face, even though bodily ease may be found there.
But when the one who is familiar and beloved to it calls to it, let it at once go to him in fear.
This is the good and measured help that the soul's anger gives toward wisdom.
For such a one becomes implacable, opposed to its enemies, when it never tolerates the love of anything harmful,
but pursues evil desire like a wolf and strangles it.
And such is the benefit of anger for those who know how to use it with understanding.
For the other powers of the soul too, according to the way they are used, prove either good or evil for the one who possesses them,
just as with the soul's power of desire: whoever uses it for the wills of the flesh and for those defiled pleasures is abominable and defiled,
but whoever turns it toward the love of God and toward desire for the eternal good things is to be emulated and is blessed.
Again, as for the power of reasoning: whoever uses it well is wise and knowledgeable, but one whose mind is sharpened to harm his neighbor is wicked and an evildoer.
Now therefore, O brothers, let us not make the means and instruments that the Creator gave us for the salvation of our souls into causes of sin.
For as the other powers are, so also is anger: when it is stirred up at the time it ought to be and in the way it ought to be,
it brings the soul to courage and endurance; but if it arises outside its proper order, it turns into madness.
For this reason the Psalmist also teaches us, "In your anger do not sin," and the Lord too makes the one who is angry without cause liable to judgment;
but he does not make the proper use of anger improper, as it is like a good medicine.
For the word that says, "I will put enmity between you and the serpent," and again,
"Be enemies to the Midianites": this teaches us the use of anger, as of a weapon.
For this reason Moses too, who was the meekest of all men, when he was exacting vengeance for the idolatry, directed the hands of the Levites to the killing of their brothers, for he said,
"Let each man put his sword on his thigh, and pass from gate to gate, and go back through the camp, and let each man kill his brother and each man his neighbor."
And in the same place, a little further on, it is written:
"Moses said: Fill your hands today for the Lord, each of you against his own son and his own brother, so that a blessing may be given to you."
And Phinehas, again, what justified him? Was it not his righteous wrath against those fornicators, he who was calm and meek in all other things?
When he saw the fornication of Zimri and the Midianite woman, how it was being committed openly and shamelessly by those who did not even cover their shame,
he could not bear that indecent sight, but made proper use of anger, for he drove his spear through both of them.
And Samuel: did he not, with righteous wrath, bring into the midst and kill Agag, king of Amalek, who had not been killed by Saul, contrary to the command of God?
Thus anger often becomes an inducer [?] of good deeds.
And again, the zealous Elijah, the four hundred and fifty priests of Shame and the other four hundred of the grove, who ate at the table of Jezebel,
he slaughtered with good and proper anger, for the benefit of all Israel. But you rage against your brother without cause; and how is it not without cause?
For the doer of the deed is someone else, and you have become angry on account of another, and you do the deed of dogs, who bite the stones and do not touch the one who throws them.
For the one through whom it is done is to be pitied and not hated, but the one who does it is the one to be hated.
Turn your anger against him, against that murderer, who is the father of lies, who is the doer of sin.
But for your brother rather feel pity, for if he remains in that sin along with the devil, he will be given over to the eternal fire.
And just as the names of anger and wrath are distinct, so too their signs are distinct:
for anger is like a kindling and a sudden boiling up of the passion, whereas wrath is a lasting grief and a firm impulse against the one who does evil.
When the soul sets about doing evil, it must be understood that people sin in both of these ways:
either they are roused fiercely and like fire against those who distress them, or with guile and wickedness they seek to do evil to them; and both of these must be fled.
And if you ask me how it may come about that this passion is not roused improperly, listen and I will tell you,
for if from the very beginning you train yourselves in that humility which the Lord taught us by word and deed, as when he said:
"Whoever wishes to be great among you, let him be the lowest of all," and again, how meekly and calmly he bore the one who struck him on the cheek.
For the King and Creator of heaven and earth, who is worshiped by all creatures visible and invisible,
He who "upholds all things by the word of his power" did not cast that man down alive into hell,
so that the earth would open and swallow up that lawless man. Instead, see how gently he teaches him:
"If I have spoken evil, bear witness to the evil; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?"
For if you too accustom yourself to count yourself the last of all, according to the Lord's commandment, when would you ever become enraged, as though you were being insulted beneath your dignity?
For consider this: if a little child insults you, you make the insult a cause for laughter, and if you are insulted by someone deranged and raving, you pity him all the more and do not hate him.
Do you see that it is not the words that disturb you, but your own mind: your contempt for the speaker and the fact that you consider yourself great?
But if you wipe both of these from your mind, all those insults will scatter uselessly in the air.
"Cease, then, from wrath and forsake anger," so that you may be saved from that wrath which "is revealed from heaven against all the lawlessness and wickedness of men."
For if with a mind made wise you are able to cut off that bitter root of anger, you will pull up many passions along with it.
For guile and duplicity and suspicion and unbelief and malice and evil plotting and arrogance and vehemence and the whole host of all such evils are shoots of this wickedness.
Let us not, then, bring into ourselves so evil a sickness of the soul, a darkness of the mind, an estrangement from God,
an alienation of kinship, a beginning of battle, an accomplisher of trials, an evil demon that is born within our very souls,
and that, like a shameless resident of the household, takes possession of everything and does not allow the Holy Spirit to enter into us.
For where there is enmity, wrath, anger, envy, and strife, which give birth to unquenchable turmoil in the soul, there the Spirit of meekness cannot rest.

Let us therefore listen to the command of the holy apostle Paul, and let us wipe away from ourselves all wrath and anger and clamor, together with all evils, and let us become kind and gentle toward one another.
And let us await that blessed hope which the Lord promised to the meek, for "Blessed are the meek,
for they shall inherit the earth," through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
